questions.prompt: What is light?
choices: A form of energy and an electromagnetic wave
questions.explanation: Light is electromagnetic radiation that carries energy.

questions.prompt: What does light need to travel through empty space?
questions.explanation: Electromagnetic waves can travel through a vacuum.

questions.prompt: What is the speed of light in vacuum?
questions.explanation: The speed of light is approximately 3 × 10^8 m/s.

questions.prompt: Which symbol represents the speed of light?
questions.explanation: c represents the speed of light in vacuum.

questions.prompt: Which equation relates speed, frequency, and wavelength?
questions.explanation: The wave equation is c = fλ.

questions.prompt: What is wavelength?
questions.explanation: Wavelength is the distance from one crest to the next.

questions.prompt: What is frequency measured in?
questions.explanation: Frequency is measured in hertz (Hz), meaning cycles per second.

questions.prompt: What does a larger amplitude of visible light generally mean?
questions.explanation: Greater amplitude corresponds to greater brightness.

questions.prompt: Light is classified as what type of wave?
questions.explanation: The electric and magnetic fields vibrate perpendicular to the direction of travel.

questions.prompt: In an electromagnetic wave, the electric and magnetic fields are:
choices: At right angles to each other
In the same direction as travel
questions.explanation: The electric and magnetic fields are perpendicular to each other and to the direction of travel.

questions.prompt: Which phenomenon is best explained by the ray model?
questions.explanation: Reflection can be described using rays.

questions.prompt: What is the law of reflection?
questions.explanation: The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.

questions.prompt: What causes refraction?
questions.explanation: Light bends because its speed changes when it enters a different medium.

questions.prompt: Which equation gives refractive index?
questions.explanation: n = c/v.

questions.prompt: When light enters glass from air, its frequency:
questions.explanation: Frequency does not change when light enters another medium.

questions.prompt: When light enters glass from air, its wavelength generally:
questions.explanation: The speed decreases while frequency stays constant, so wavelength decreases.

questions.prompt: Which phenomenon separates white light into different colours?
questions.explanation: Dispersion occurs because different wavelengths bend by different amounts.

questions.prompt: Which phenomenon produces bright and dark fringes?
questions.explanation: Interference produces regions of constructive and destructive interference.

questions.prompt: Diffraction is the:
choices: Spreading of waves around edges or through narrow gaps
questions.explanation: Diffraction causes waves to spread after passing through small openings or around obstacles.

questions.prompt: What does polarisation show about light?
questions.explanation: Only transverse waves can be polarised.

questions.prompt: Which is the correct order of the electromagnetic spectrum from lowest to highest frequency?
choices: Gamma, X-ray, UV, visible, IR, microwave, radio
Radio, microwave, IR, visible, UV, X-ray, gamma
Radio, IR, microwave, visible, X-ray, UV, gamma
Visible, radio, microwave, IR, UV, gamma, X-ray
questions.explanation: Frequency increases from radio waves toward gamma rays.

questions.prompt: Which electromagnetic wave has the longest wavelength?
questions.explanation: Radio waves have the longest wavelengths.

questions.prompt: Which electromagnetic wave has the highest frequency?
questions.explanation: Gamma rays have the highest frequencies.

questions.prompt: Which has the greatest photon energy?
questions.explanation: Photon energy increases with frequency: E = hf.

questions.prompt: Which visible colour has greater photon energy?
choices: Red and blue have the same energy
questions.explanation: Blue has a higher frequency and therefore greater photon energy.

questions.prompt: What is the photon energy equation?
questions.explanation: Photon energy is E = hf.

questions.prompt: Which equation can calculate photon energy using wavelength in nm?
What is a photon?
questions.explanation: A photon is a discrete packet of electromagnetic energy.

questions.prompt: What is a blackbody?
choices: An object that reflects all radiation
An ideal object that absorbs all incident radiation
An object that emits only visible light
questions.explanation: A blackbody absorbs all radiation falling on it.

questions.prompt: What determines the radiation emitted by an ideal blackbody?
questions.explanation: Blackbody radiation depends only on temperature.

questions.prompt: As the temperature of a blackbody increases, the peak wavelength:
questions.explanation: Hotter objects peak at shorter wavelengths.

questions.prompt: Which object is approximately a blackbody?
questions.explanation: The Sun is a good approximate blackbody.

questions.prompt: A hotter star generally appears:
questions.explanation: Higher temperatures shift the peak toward shorter, bluer wavelengths.

questions.prompt: What was the ultraviolet catastrophe?
choices: Classical theory predicting unlimited energy at short wavelengths
UV light being unable to travel
questions.explanation: Classical physics predicted increasing energy toward very short wavelengths, contrary to experiment.

questions.prompt: Who introduced the idea that energy is emitted in discrete packets?
questions.explanation: Planck proposed energy quanta to explain blackbody radiation.

questions.prompt: What does E = hf represent in blackbody/quantum theory?
questions.explanation: Energy is quantised in packets with energy hf.

questions.prompt: What is the photoelectric effect?
choices: Light knocking electrons out of a metal
questions.explanation: The photoelectric effect is the emission of electrons from a metal due to light.

questions.prompt: What determines the maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons?
questions.explanation: KEmax = hf − φ, so frequency determines photon energy and electron kinetic energy.

questions.prompt: What determines how many photoelectrons are emitted?
choices: Intensity, when frequency is above threshold
questions.explanation: Greater intensity means more photons and therefore more emitted electrons.

questions.prompt: What is the work function?
choices: Minimum energy needed to remove an electron from a metal
Energy of a photon after emission
questions.explanation: The work function φ is the minimum energy needed to free an electron.

questions.prompt: What is threshold frequency?
choices: The minimum frequency needed to eject electrons
The frequency of visible light only
questions.explanation: Below the threshold frequency, photoemission does not occur.

questions.prompt: Which equation represents the photoelectric effect?
questions.explanation: Photon energy first supplies the work function; the remainder becomes kinetic energy.

questions.prompt: What is stopping potential?
choices: Voltage that accelerates the fastest electrons
Reverse voltage just sufficient to stop the fastest photoelectrons
questions.explanation: The stopping potential prevents even the fastest photoelectrons from reaching the collector.

questions.prompt: What happens if light frequency is below the threshold frequency?
choices: More electrons are emitted if brightness increases
questions.explanation: Each photon lacks enough energy to overcome the work function.

questions.prompt: What did de Broglie propose?
choices: Only light can behave as a wave
Matter particles can also behave as waves
questions.explanation: de Broglie proposed matter waves with λ = h/p.

questions.prompt: What is the de Broglie wavelength equation?
questions.explanation: Matter-wave wavelength is inversely proportional to momentum.

questions.prompt: If a particle's momentum increases, its de Broglie wavelength:
questions.explanation: λ = h/p.

questions.prompt: Which experiment demonstrates electron diffraction?
questions.explanation: Davisson-Germer demonstrated electron diffraction. The study guide marks this experiment as NOT in the exam.

questions.prompt: Which is evidence that light behaves as a wave?
questions.explanation: Interference is a wave phenomenon.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes wave-particle duality?
choices: Light is always only a wave
Matter is always only a particle
Both light and matter can show wave and particle behaviour
Waves and particles are completely unrelated
questions.explanation:
Experiments show both light and matter have wave-like and particle-like behaviour.
Part 2 — 50 True/False Questions

questions.prompt: Light can travel through a vacuum.
questions.explanation: Electromagnetic waves do not require a material medium.

questions.prompt: Sound and light both require a material medium.
questions.explanation: Sound needs a medium, but light can travel through vacuum.

questions.prompt: The speed of light in vacuum is approximately 3 × 10^8 m/s.
questions.explanation: This is the value of c.

questions.prompt: Light is a longitudinal wave.
questions.explanation: Light is a transverse electromagnetic wave.

questions.prompt: The electric and magnetic fields of an electromagnetic wave are perpendicular to each other.
questions.explanation: They oscillate at right angles to each other.

questions.prompt: Frequency is measured in metres.
questions.explanation: Frequency is measured in hertz.

questions.prompt: Wavelength is measured in metres.
questions.explanation: The SI unit of wavelength is metre.

questions.prompt: The amplitude of visible light is related to its brightness.
questions.explanation: Greater amplitude corresponds to brighter light.

questions.prompt: In vacuum, all electromagnetic waves travel at the same speed.
questions.explanation: All EM radiation travels at 3 × 10^8 m/s in vacuum.

questions.prompt: Radio waves have a shorter wavelength than gamma rays.
questions.explanation: Radio waves have the longest wavelengths.

questions.prompt: Gamma rays have the highest frequency in the electromagnetic spectrum.
questions.explanation: Gamma rays are at the highest-frequency end.

questions.prompt: Infrared has a higher frequency than visible light.
questions.explanation: Infrared has lower frequency than visible light.

questions.prompt: X-rays have greater photon energy than visible light.
questions.explanation: X-rays have higher frequency, so E = hf gives greater energy.

questions.prompt: Red photons have more energy than blue photons.
questions.explanation: Blue has a higher frequency and therefore higher energy.

questions.prompt: Photon energy increases when wavelength decreases.
questions.explanation: E = hc/λ.

questions.prompt: Reflection is described using the wave model only.
questions.explanation: Reflection is one of the properties described by the ray model in the guide.

questions.prompt: The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.
questions.explanation: This is the law of reflection.

questions.prompt: Refraction occurs because light changes speed between media.
questions.explanation: The speed changes when light enters a different medium.

questions.prompt: Light's frequency changes when it enters glass.
questions.explanation: Frequency stays constant when crossing the boundary.

questions.prompt: Light's wavelength can change when it enters glass.
questions.explanation: The speed changes while frequency stays constant.

questions.prompt: Polarisation proves that light is transverse.
questions.explanation: Only transverse waves can be polarised.

questions.prompt: Diffraction is the spreading of waves through narrow gaps or around edges.
questions.explanation: That is the definition of diffraction.

questions.prompt: Interference can create bright and dark fringes.
questions.explanation: Constructive and destructive interference produce the fringes.

questions.prompt: Dispersion causes white light to separate into colours.
questions.explanation: Different wavelengths bend by different amounts.

questions.prompt: A refractive index of 1.5 means light travels faster than in vacuum.
questions.explanation: n = c/v, so n > 1 means the speed is lower than c.

questions.prompt: A blackbody reflects all radiation falling on it.
questions.explanation: An ideal blackbody absorbs all incident radiation.

questions.prompt: Blackbody radiation depends on the object's temperature.
questions.explanation: Temperature determines the emitted radiation spectrum.

questions.prompt: A hotter blackbody emits more total radiation.
questions.explanation: Increasing temperature increases the total emitted energy.

questions.prompt: A hotter blackbody's peak shifts toward longer wavelengths.
questions.explanation: The peak shifts toward shorter wavelengths.

questions.prompt: A blue-hot object is generally hotter than a red-hot object.
questions.explanation: Higher temperature shifts radiation toward shorter wavelengths.

questions.prompt: The Sun is approximately a blackbody.
questions.explanation: Its radiation closely resembles blackbody radiation.

questions.prompt: Wien's displacement law is required for the exam according to the study guide.
questions.explanation: The guide specifically marks Wien's law as “NOT in Exam.”

questions.prompt: Stefan-Boltzmann's law is marked “NOT in Exam.”
questions.explanation: The study guide explicitly excludes it.

questions.prompt: Planck proposed that energy is emitted continuously.
questions.explanation: Planck proposed that energy is emitted and absorbed in discrete packets.

questions.prompt: The ultraviolet catastrophe was correctly predicted by classical physics.
questions.explanation: Classical theory predicted an incorrect infinite increase at short wavelengths.

questions.prompt: The photoelectric effect involves electrons being emitted from a metal.
questions.explanation: Light can eject electrons from a suitable metal.

questions.prompt: Increasing brightness can make below-threshold-frequency light eject electrons.
questions.explanation: If each photon lacks enough energy, increasing the number of photons does not solve the problem.

questions.prompt: Higher-frequency light gives each photon more energy.
questions.explanation: E = hf.

questions.prompt: Increasing light intensity above threshold usually increases the number of emitted electrons.
questions.explanation: Greater intensity means more photons hitting the surface.

questions.prompt: Increasing intensity always increases the maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons.
questions.explanation: Frequency determines maximum kinetic energy; intensity mainly changes the number of electrons.

questions.prompt: The work function is the minimum energy needed to remove an electron.
questions.explanation: That is the definition of work function.

questions.prompt: Threshold frequency is the minimum frequency required for photoemission.
questions.explanation: Below it, photoemission does not occur.

questions.prompt: Photoelectrons can take several seconds to leave the metal after illumination.
questions.explanation: The photoelectric effect occurs almost immediately.

questions.prompt: Stopping potential is a reverse voltage.
questions.explanation: It opposes the motion of photoelectrons toward the collector.

questions.prompt: The maximum kinetic energy is given by KEmax = hf − φ.
questions.explanation: Photon energy is divided between overcoming the work function and electron kinetic energy.

questions.prompt: de Broglie proposed that particles have wave properties.
questions.explanation: Matter waves have wavelength λ = h/p.

questions.prompt: A larger momentum gives a longer de Broglie wavelength.
questions.explanation: λ = h/p, so larger momentum means shorter wavelength.

questions.prompt: A moving electron can have a wavelength.
questions.explanation: Electrons have matter-wave properties.

questions.prompt: A cricket ball has a noticeable de Broglie wavelength.
questions.explanation: Its large momentum gives an extremely tiny wavelength.

questions.prompt: Wave-particle duality applies only to light.
questions.explanation:
Matter particles such as electrons also show wave-particle duality.
Part 3 — 50 Calculation MCQs
Use these constants where needed:
c = 3 × 10^8 m/s
h = 6.63 × 10^-34 J·s
h = 4.14 × 10^-15 eV·s
E(eV) = 1240/λ(nm)
1 eV = 1.6 × 10^-19 J
1 nm = 10^-9 m
n = c/v
λ = h/p
p = mv
λ = 1.23/√V nm for an electron accelerated through V volts.

questions.prompt: A light wave has a wavelength of 600 nm. What is its frequency?
What is the wavelength of a 100 MHz radio wave?
A light wave has a frequency of 6 × 10^14 Hz. What is its wavelength?
What is the frequency of 700 nm red light?
Light travels through glass with refractive index 1.5. What is its speed?
Light of wavelength 600 nm enters glass with n = 1.5. What is its wavelength in glass?
questions.explanation:
Frequency stays the same, so:
λglass = λair/n = 600/1.5 = 400 nm.

questions.prompt: If the frequency of light is 5 × 10^14 Hz, what is its wavelength in vacuum?
What is the energy of a 620 nm photon?
What is the energy of a 400 nm photon?
What is the energy of a 100 nm photon?
questions.explanation:
E = 1240/100 = 12.4 eV.
Correction: 12.4 eV is the calculated result, so the correct choice is B.

questions.prompt: What is the energy of a 0.1 nm X-ray photon?
A photon has energy 4 eV. Approximately what is its wavelength?
A photon has wavelength 500 nm. What is its energy?
What is the energy in joules of a 2 eV photon?
A blackbody is at 727°C. What is its temperature in Kelvin?
A blackbody has a temperature of 1000 K. What is approximately its peak wavelength using Wien's law?
questions.explanation:
λmax = 2.898 × 10^-3 / 1000
= 2.898 × 10^-6 m.
Note: The study guide marks Wien's law as NOT in Exam.

questions.prompt: A star peaks at 483 nm. What is its approximate temperature using Wien's law?
Which temperature is hotter?
questions.explanation: Higher Kelvin temperature means a hotter object.

questions.prompt: If a blackbody's temperature increases, its peak wavelength moves toward:
questions.explanation: Wien's law shows λmax is inversely proportional to temperature.

questions.prompt: A metal has a work function of 2.3 eV. What is the threshold wavelength?
questions.explanation:
λ0 = 1240/φ
λ0 = 1240/2.3 ≈ 539 nm.
Correction: The correct answer is C, 539 nm, approximately 540 nm.

questions.prompt: Sodium has a work function of 2.3 eV. A 400 nm photon hits it. What is the maximum kinetic energy?
questions.explanation:
Photon energy:
E = 1240/400 = 3.1 eV
KEmax = 3.1 − 2.3 = 0.8 eV.

questions.prompt: A metal has a work function of 4.7 eV. What is its approximate threshold wavelength?
A 500 nm photon hits a metal with work function 2 eV. What is the maximum kinetic energy?
questions.explanation:
E = 1240/500 = 2.48 eV
KEmax = 2.48 − 2 = 0.48 eV.
Correction: The correct answer is A, 0.48 eV.

questions.prompt: A photon has frequency 8 × 10^14 Hz. What is its energy?
Sodium has a work function of 2.3 eV. If the photon energy is 3.3 eV, what is the maximum kinetic energy?
If the maximum kinetic energy of a photoelectron is 1.0 eV, what is the stopping potential?
questions.explanation: Numerically, electron kinetic energy in eV equals stopping potential in volts.

questions.prompt: A photon has frequency 5 × 10^14 Hz. What is its energy in eV?
A metal has a work function of 3 eV. Light provides photons of 2 eV. What happens?
questions.explanation: Photon energy is less than the work function.

questions.prompt: A metal has a work function of 2 eV. Photons have energy 5 eV. What is KEmax?
questions.explanation: KEmax = 5 − 2 = 3 eV.

questions.prompt: What happens to the maximum kinetic energy if the light frequency increases?
questions.explanation: KEmax = hf − φ, so increasing f increases KEmax.

questions.prompt: An electron has a mass of 9.1 × 10^-31 kg and speed 1 × 10^6 m/s. What is its momentum?
An electron has momentum 9.1 × 10^-25 kg m/s. What is its de Broglie wavelength?
A particle has mass 0.15 kg and speed 30 m/s. What is its momentum?
What is the de Broglie wavelength of the particle in Question 133?
An electron is accelerated through 100 V. What is its approximate wavelength?
An electron is accelerated through 10,000 V. What is its approximate wavelength?
An electron is accelerated through 25 V. What is its approximate wavelength?
An electron has a de Broglie wavelength of 0.123 nm. Approximately what accelerating voltage produced it?
A double-slit experiment uses light of wavelength 600 nm. The screen is 1 m away and slit separation is 0.2 mm. What is the fringe spacing?
In a double-slit experiment, what happens to fringe spacing if wavelength increases?
questions.explanation: β = λD/d, so fringe spacing is directly proportional to wavelength.

questions.prompt: In a double-slit experiment, if slit separation increases, fringe spacing:
questions.explanation: β = λD/d, so increasing d decreases β.

A photon has energy 3.1 eV. What is its approximate wavelength?
A metal has work function 2.1 eV. What is its threshold wavelength?
A 500 nm photon hits a metal with work function 2.1 eV. What is the maximum kinetic energy?
What stopping potential corresponds to a maximum kinetic energy of 0.38 eV?
questions.explanation: KEmax(eV) has the same numerical value as V0 in volts.
